caption:
Meta's updated commercial terms, effective October 30, let it scrape websites tied to business accounts, news publishers included.
Legal experts told Nieman Lab the wording would let Meta train AI on that content. Meta says nothing changes in how it crawls.

Should AI companies have to pay news sites to train on their work?

slides.headline: Meta just gave itself permission to *scrape news sites* for AI, legal experts say

slides.heading: The *fine print*
paras: Meta's updated commercial terms take effect October 30. They cover business accounts that run Facebook pages, Instagram profiles, ads or WhatsApp channels.
Account holders authorize Meta to use web scrapers and bots on their sites, and to use that content to develop and train its products.

slides.heading: Lawyers *sound the alarm*
paras: Cornell law professor James Grimmelmann told Nieman Lab it "clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites."
Attorney Matt Topic said publishers should assume it is enforceable. The terms offer no opt-out except to stop using Meta for business.

slides.heading: Meta's *answer*
paras: A Meta spokesperson said the update only gathers crawling language that was already spread across its other terms.
Meta says it will not change how it crawls publishers, and site owners can still limit access with robots.txt.

slides.heading: Europe's publishers *fight back*
paras: The European Publishers Council wants the European Commission to step in. Its director, Angela Mills Wade, said Meta "cannot simply write itself permission to take that work."

paras.t: Publishers want to decide how their journalism is used, and get paid for it.

slides.hook: Meta's new terms kick in October 30. Follow to see whether news publishers fight them.
